## Smooth $\mu(x)$, and say what you assumed {#sec-smooth}

StatHarbor Analytics, *Smoothing and Nonparametric Methods*, uses "nonparametric" for a curve that is not fixed in advance as a short formula. Complexity may grow with $n$. The structure that replaces the formula is smoothness, locality, or a penalty.

::: assumption
$$
Y = \mu(x) + \varepsilon, \qquad \mathbb{E}(\varepsilon \mid x) = 0.
$$
Their $f(x)$ is this $\mu(x)$. A straight line $\mu(x) = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is efficient when it is close to the curve, and biased when the curve bends.
:::

[Angelino and Marcone](https://www.sib.swiss/training/course/20260907_ADDMG) make the same opening: a linear model is easy to interpret, and the straight line is often an approximation.

## One path, rising flexibility {#sec-smooth-map}

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 11
%%| fig-height: 2.2
flowchart LR
  line["straight $$\mu$$"] --> local["LOESS"]
  local --> gcv["GCV"]
  gcv --> knots["knots"]
  knots --> penalty["penalty"]
  penalty --> gam["GAM"]
```

Left to right: a straight mean, a local polynomial, a bandwidth chosen by GCV, a spline with knots, a spline with a penalty, then one smooth per covariate.

Each step spends a tuning choice: a bandwidth, a set of knots, or a penalty. The last step is how that choice survives more than one covariate.

## Flexibility spends variance {#sec-bias-variance}

At a point $x_0$, StatHarbor decomposes the error in the curve:

$$
\mathbb{E}\big(\hat\mu(x_0) - \mu(x_0)\big)^2
  = \mathrm{Var}\big(\hat\mu(x_0)\big)
  + \mathrm{Bias}\big(\hat\mu(x_0)\big)^2.
$$

Predicting a new $Y$ adds $\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon \mid x_0)$ on top of that. More flexibility usually cuts the bias and raises the variance. A small bandwidth is the noisy end. A large bandwidth is the oversmoothed end.

## A kernel is a local bump {#sec-kde}

Before the regression, the same idea estimates a density. Each observation contributes a bump of width $h$:

$$
\hat f_h(x) = \frac{1}{nh}\sum_{i=1}^{n} K\!\left(\frac{x_i - x}{h}\right).
$$

They name four kernels: Gaussian, Epanechnikov, uniform, and triangular. Bandwidth matters far more than which of those four you pick.

::: {.notes}
For a Gaussian kernel, Silverman's rule of thumb is $\hat h \approx 1.06\,\hat\sigma\, n^{-1/5}$. They say it is often adequate for a roughly unimodal symmetric density, and that it fails for a skewed, multimodal, or heavy-tailed density. The AMISE-optimal bandwidth shrinks as $n^{-1/5}$: nonparametric rates are slower than a well-specified parametric rate.
:::

## Local weights for $\mu(x_0)$ {#sec-nw}

::: model
$$
\hat\mu(x_0) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i(x_0)\, Y_i, \qquad \sum_i w_i(x_0) = 1.
$$
Nadaraya–Watson sets $w_i$ from $K((x_i-x_0)/h)$. That fit is a local constant: a weighted average of nearby $Y_i$.
:::

Near the edge of $x$ the window is one-sided, so a local constant is pulled inward and the curve flattens. That boundary bias is why the next fit is local linear.

## Fit a line in the window {#sec-local-linear}

At $x_0$, minimise the weighted residual sum of squares of a line in $(x_i - x_0)$. The fitted value is the local intercept.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="1"} Degree 0 is the local constant, Nadaraya–Watson.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="2"} Degree 1 is local linear. StatHarbor's default: less boundary bias, still local.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="3"} Degree 2 is local quadratic.

Angelino and Marcone's LOESS often uses the quadratic. The two sources agree on the algorithm and differ on the default degree.

## LOESS is that regression, with a span {#sec-loess}

::: model
LOESS is local polynomial regression with a nearest-neighbour window. The span is a proportion of the sample, in $(0, 1]$. StatHarbor's example is $0.3$. The window widens where $x$ is sparse. The usual weight is the tricube kernel.
:::

[]{.fragment fragment-index="1"} Angelino and Marcone: choose the span, find the nearest neighbours, weight them, fit the local polynomial.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="2"} The fit does not start from a named formula, and it does not return one.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="3"} It wants a large, densely sampled $x$. Their use is exploratory smoothing of a scatterplot.

## Robust LOESS reweights large residuals {#sec-loess-robust}

StatHarbor's robust LOESS protects the local fit from a few extreme $Y_i$.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="1"} Fit an initial LOESS curve.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="2"} Compute residuals.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="3"} Downweight unusually large residuals.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="4"} Refit with both the proximity weights and those robustness weights.

The span is still chosen separately. The next slide is that choice, for a linear smoother. Robust weights take the fit outside the linear-smoother case their GCV formula assumes.

## GCV chooses the bandwidth {#sec-gcv}

A linear smoother is $\hat{\mathbf{Y}} = \mathbf{S}\mathbf{Y}$. Leave-one-out cross-validation refits $n$ times. Generalised cross-validation approximates it:

$$
\mathrm{GCV}(h)
  = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_i\big(Y_i - \hat\mu(x_i)\big)^2}{\big(1 - \mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S})/n\big)^2}.
$$

The bandwidth that minimises GCV is their predictive choice. The same criterion, with the penalty weight in place of $h$, is how they tune a smoothing spline. Kernel choice stays secondary.

## A global polynomial moves the whole curve

Angelino and Marcone extend the line by powers of $x$. A quadratic uses $x$ and $x^2$. They stop at degree 3 or 4: higher powers become strange near the ends of $x$. StatHarbor's matching warning is that a local change then alters the fit far away.

[Lopez-Ayala, Riley, Collins, and Zimmermann](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2024-082440) add fractional polynomials: powers that need not be whole numbers. The function is still defined on the whole range of $x$, so a pile of values in one tail can distort the shape everywhere.

## A regression spline spends its flexibility at knots {#sec-reg-spline}

::: model
Knots $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_K$ cut $x$ into intervals. A cubic piece is fitted in each, with $f$, $f'$, and $f''$ continuous at the knots. The truncated-power basis is $\beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2 + \beta_3 x^3 + \sum_k \theta_k (x-\xi_k)_+^3$.
:::

The analyst chooses how many knots, and where. A common default is the quantiles of $x$. Angelino and Marcone: after the continuity constraints, each added knot costs about one degree of freedom, and the spline is most flexible where the knots are dense. A step function, their piecewise constant, misses the trend unless the cut-points are real breaks. That is the [dichotomisation](#sec-dichotomise) case.

## B-splines span the same curves {#sec-b-spline}

The truncated-power basis is clear and numerically unstable. A B-spline basis spans the same spline space with local support: each basis function is zero outside a few intervals. The design matrix is sparse, and the fit is better conditioned. Software prefers this basis. The knots are still chosen by hand. The next smoother removes that choice and penalises roughness instead.

## A penalty replaces the knot count {#sec-smooth-spline}

::: model
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(Y_i - \mu(x_i)\big)^2
  + \lambda \int \big(\mu''(t)\big)^2\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$
The first term is fidelity. The integral is curvature. Here $\lambda$ is the penalty weight, not a Poisson rate and not a relative intensity. Large $\lambda$ forces a smooth curve. Small $\lambda$ allows a wiggly one. A straight line has $\mu'' = 0$, so the penalty does not forbid a bend. It discourages a bend the data do not support.
:::

## The solution is a natural cubic spline {#sec-spline-theorem}

::: theorem
The minimiser, over a suitable class of functions, is a natural cubic spline with a knot at every observed $x_i$.
:::

Angelino and Marcone list the same properties: piecewise cubic, knots at the distinct $x_i$, continuous first and second derivatives, and linear beyond the extreme knots. An infinite-dimensional penalty problem becomes a finite spline. In matrix form it is penalised least squares, the ridge pattern $(\mathbf{N}^{\top}\mathbf{N} + \lambda\boldsymbol{\Omega})^{-1}\mathbf{N}^{\top}\mathbf{Y}$.

Effective degrees of freedom are $\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_\lambda)$. As $\lambda \to \infty$ the fit approaches a straight line. As $\lambda \to 0$ it approaches interpolation. GCV, with $\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_\lambda)$ in the denominator, chooses $\lambda$.

## Restricted cubics are the applied form of that constraint {#sec-rcs}

[The BMJ guide](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2024-082440) calls the natural spline a restricted cubic spline: cubics between the inner knots, and a straight line before the first knot and after the last. The tails, where points are few and outliers bite, stay stable. With $k$ knots the model spends $k-1$ degrees of freedom. Three knots, their usual start, sit at the 10th, 50th, and 90th percentiles of $x$. Three to five knots is the range they recommend, and AIC can choose the number. The exact quantile locations rarely change the curve.

Coefficients of a spline are not the summary. The partial-effect plot is.

## The curve can rise twice {#sec-rcs-glucose}

On the meningitis data, CSF glucose against bacterial meningitis: a straight line, and a cut at 62 mg/dL, both miss the second rise at high glucose that the three-knot restricted cubic shows.

::: assumption
Do not categorise a continuous covariate, and do not assume a straight line, whether the aim is to predict, explain, or describe. Spend degrees of freedom first on the covariates that matter. Choosing the shape by eye, before the fit, spends phantom degrees of freedom and makes the interval too narrow.
:::

## A neighbourhood empties as dimension grows {#sec-curse}

Local methods need nearby observations. As the number of covariates grows, those neighbourhoods empty, and "local" stops meaning a small window. Naive multivariate smoothing breaks down. The practical compromise is an additive mean: one smooth per covariate, estimated as a one-dimensional problem.

## A GAM is an additive smooth on the link {#sec-gam}

::: model
$$
g(\mu) = \beta_0 + s_1(x_1) + \cdots + s_p(x_p),
\qquad \mu = \mathbb{E}(Y \mid \mathbf{x}).
$$
A logistic GAM uses the logit. A Poisson GAM uses the log. Each $s_j$ is a one-dimensional smoother. Backfitting cycles through partial residuals until the smooths settle.
:::

Because the mean is a sum, each $\hat s_j$ has its own plot: a line, a threshold, a saturation, a U-shape. StatHarbor's distinction: that plot is the component, not a black-box importance score. The BMJ guide names `mgcv` for this fit, beside `rms` for the restricted cubic, and treats GAMs and LOESS as the alternatives to fractional polynomials and splines.

## Which smoother for which task {#sec-which-smoother}

[]{.fragment fragment-index="1"} Exploratory visualisation: LOESS.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="2"} Density estimation: kernel density estimation.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="3"} A stable smooth regression in one covariate: smoothing splines.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="4"} Moderate flexibility with the basis written down: regression splines, including restricted cubics and B-splines.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="5"} Several covariates, with a plot per covariate: a generalised additive model.

## Four controls on the flexibility {#sec-smooth-takeaways}

[]{.fragment fragment-index="1"} Smoothness or locality replaces a rigid global formula.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="2"} The control is a bandwidth, a penalty, or the size of the basis.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="3"} Choosing that control is part of the performance, not a detail after the fit.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="4"} In higher dimensions, an additive structure, or some other structure, becomes necessary.

::: {.notes}
StatHarbor's reading list: Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman (2009), *The Elements of Statistical Learning*; Wood (2017), *Generalized Additive Models: An Introduction with R*; Wasserman (2006), *All of Nonparametric Statistics*; Fan and Gijbels (1996), *Local Polynomial Modelling and Its Applications*; Silverman (1986), *Density Estimation for Statistics and Data Analysis*; Green and Silverman (1994), *Nonparametric Regression and Generalized Linear Models*. MARS and projection pursuit are their two extensions that relax strict additivity. They mark the links to kernels and neural nets as conceptual, not equivalences.
:::
